1.x: This verse shows that Jesus doesn’t just give orders; he leads by example.”made an end of commanding”: Jesus had finished the “classroom” portion of the disciples’ training. He has given them the power, the plan, and the warnings. Now it’s time for the theory to become practice. “In their cities”: This likely refers to the cities of the Jewish people (“their” meaning the disciples’ fellow countrymen). Jesus continues to prioritize the “lost sheep of the house of Israel.” While the humanity of Jesus is walking the dusty roads of Galilee, the Deity within him (the Father) is the source of the teaching and preaching. When Jesus teaches in these cities, it is the One God of the OT finally speaking to His people face-to-face. God said in the OT that His people would one day know His name and that He would be the one speaking to them: “Therefore my people shall know my name: therefore they shall know in that day that I am he that doth speak: behold, it is I.” (Isa 52:6 KJV).

6.x: Jesus delivers a gentle but deeply searching warning to anyone (including John the Baptist) who finds the reality of His Kingdom different from their expectations. “Offended”: The Greek word for “offended” is “skandalizō” (the root of our word “scandal”). It refers to the “trigger” of a trap, the part that causes the animal to be caught. When Jesus says “not be offended,” he is saying: “Blessed is the person who doesn’t let their own preconceived ideas about who I should be become a trap that causes them to turn away from who I actually am.” John the Baptist expected a Messiah of fire and judgement. Instead, he received a Messiah of grace and healing. The “offense” is the gap between what we demand God should do and what God is actually doing. Jesus calls the person who overcomes this offense “blessed” (makarios), which signifies deep, spiritual contentment. It takes immense humility to admit: “God is doing something I don’t fully understand.” By not being “offended,” the disciple keeps their eyes on Jesus’ character rather than their own current circumstance (like John’s prison cell). This verse shows a challenge to accept the “mode” in which God chose to reveal Himself. Many people in the first century were “offended” by Jesus because he did not look or act like the “Almighty YHWH” they expected to see. They expected God to arrive in fire from the heavens; instead, He arrived in a manger and worked in a carpenter’s shop. We must not be “offended” that God took on human limitations (the Sonship). For the Father (Deity) to reconcile the world to Himself (2 Cor 5:19), He had to become a man. To reject the “Son” because he appears human is, in effect, to be offended by the Father’s chosen method of salvation. “Blessed is he, whosoever shall not be offended in me”: Jesus is telling the world: “Even though I appear as a man, I am the fullness of God. Do not let my humanity become a stumbling block to recognizing my divinity.” The humanity of Jesus is probably the greatest stumbling block for Muslims, who would not accept that the Creator of the Universe would come into the world: ‘He is Allah, [who is] One, Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He neither begets nor is born, nor is there to Him any equivalent.’ (Qur’an 112:1-4)

11.x: In terms of the “Old Covenant” era, John was the greatest. John is the peak because he stood at the very threshold of the Kingdom. This means that he was greater than Mary as well. Yet he never claimed veneration, rather he said: “He(Jesus) must increase, but I(John) must decrease” (Jn 3:30 KJV). John, Mary, and Paul understood that only Jesus deserves all devotion: “I am afraid, however, that just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ” (2 Cor 11:3 BSB). “he that is least.. Is greater than he”: This sounds like a slight to John, but it’s actually a statement about the New Covenant. Even the “least” believer today is “greater” in privilege because they live after the finished work on the Cross and have the indwelling Holy Spirit. John saw the Kingdom from the outside looking in; the believer lives inside it. Under the Old Covenant (where John stood), the Spirit came upon people. Under the New Covenant (the Kingdom), the Spirit of the Father (which is the divine Spirit of Christ) dwells within the believer. This internal union with God makes the New Covenant disciple “greater” in spiritual position than even the greatest OT prophet.

12.x: “The kingdom of heaven suffereth violence”: There are two ways of seeing this passage, depending whether “violence” refers to something positive or negative: (1) Negative: The Kingdom is being attacked. From the moment John began preaching, the “wolves” (the religious and political establishment) began trying to suppress the movement. John himself was in prison because of this violence. In this view, the “violent” are the enemies of God trying to “snatch” the Kingdom away to destroy it. Some thought-for-thought translations take this negative approach: “...the Kingdom of Heaven has been forcefully advancing, and violent people are attacking it” (NLT). (2) Positive: The Kingdom is being “stormed” by those desperate to get in. Because the message of Jesus and John was so radical, it attracted people who were willing to “push through” social norms, family expectations, and religious traditions to reach Jesus. In this view, the “violent” are those with a desperate, uncompromising faith (like the woman who touched Jesus’ garment or the friends who lowered the paralytic through the roof). Its parallel passage in Luke reads: “The law and the prophets were until John: since that time the kingdom of God is preached, and every man PRESSETH INTO IT” (Lk 16:16 KJV). So by harmonizing both passages, the sense of this verse seems to take the positive approach, which would mean something like: “The kingdom presses ahead relentlessly, and only the relentless press their way into it.”. This is why some other translations that are a little more thought-for-thought rather than strict word-for-word, like the MEV, translate this verse as: “From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven has forcefully advanced, and the strong take it by force” (MEV). Thus, again, Jesus is magnifying the difficulty of entering the kingdom of God.

13.x: Before Jesus, the Law (the Torah) and the prophets were the primary ways God communicated His Will and His promises to Israel. Jesus is essentially saying that John the Baptist represents the “finish line” of that era. The Old Era: Pointing forward to a promised Savior. The New Era: The Savior has arrived. John is the last of the old-style prophets, but he is unique because he actually got to point at the Messiah and say: “There he is.”

14.x: In the book of Malachi (the last book of the OT, written 400 years before the gospels), there was a prophecy that Elijah the prophet would return before "the great and dreadful day of the Lord” (probably referring to the destruction of the Jewish temple in 70AC). Jesus identifies John as the fulfillment of this prophecy. However, he adds the caveat: “If ye will receive it.” This is crucial because John didn’t literally reincarnate as Elijah, rather, he came in the “spirit & power” of Elijah (Lk 1:17). Accepting John as “Elijah” meant accepting that the Messianic age had begun, which required a massive shift in the listener’s worldview.

15.x: “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear”: This was Jesus’s way of saying: “This is a deep truth that requires more than just physical hearing.” He is calling for spiritual discernment. To the casual listener, John was just a guy in the desert eating locusts. To the one “with ears,” John was the herald of the King(the YHWH of the OT), signaling that the wait of the centuries was finally over.

20.x: Because these cities saw the literal power of God firsthand, their refusal to repent was considered a much more serious sin than the legendary wickedness of ancient cities. The core logic here is that revelation brings responsibility, and that eternal punishment will be different for different people.

23.x: Capernaum was Jesus’ “home base” during his Galilean ministry and still rejected Christ, therefore it faced an even greater condemnation. Rejecting Christ’s signs & miracles was such a serious offense that Jesus considers it worse than Sodom’s gross wickedness.

24.x: The word for “more tolerable” is anektoteron, which literally means “more bearable” or “easier to endure.” Jesus is teaching that while all sin is serious, there are degrees of accountability. Sodom sinned in relative ignorance of the Messiah, while Capernaum sinned while looking at the Messiah. Jesus isn’t just venting frustration; he is issuing warning against spiritual indifference. To see the “mighty works” of God and simply say “that’s nice” while remaining unchanged is, in Jesus’ view, a more dangerous state than being a notorious sinner who never heard the truth.

25.x: Jesus draws a sharp contrast between two types of people: (1) The Wise and Prudent (synetōn in Greek): This refers to those who rely on their own intellectual prowess, academic degrees, or social status to grasp spiritual truths. In Jesus’ day, these were often the scribes and Pharisees who knew the Law inside and out but failed to recognize the Messiah standing right in front of them. (2) Bases (nēpiois in Greek): This literally means “infants” or “untaught ones.” It refers to those who are humble, simple-hearted, and aware of their own need for a teacher. The point is that God does not reveal Himself through the “climb” of human intellect, but through the “gift” of divine revelation to the humble.

** This verse challenges “Intellectual Elitism.” If Jesus thanks the Father for hiding the truth from the “wise” (the academically elite of his day) and giving it to “babes” (uneducated fishermen and outcasts), it stands as a direct rebuke to any system that claims academic intelligence or high office is the requirement for knowing God. This passage suggests that a simple believer with a humble heart can often perceive the heart of the gospel more clearly than a scholar who lacks faith. As Paul later writes: "But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise." (1 Cor 1:27 KJV). This goes in direct contradiction to Catholic teaching that maintains the Magisterium (the teaching office) as the only and final authority on interpreting dogma. They claim to be the only ones with the authority to interpret Scripture, yet they don’t even do their job. Up until today, the Catholic Church has only infallibly interpreted a handful of passages, such as Matthew 16:18 (in connection to Peter and the papacy), John 3:5 (in connection with the necessity of baptism), Luke 22:32 (in connection with Peter’s role as an infallible Pope), 1 Corinthians 11:27-29 (in connection with worthy reception of the Eucharist) or John 6 to support Transubstantiation. But ask a Catholic about the meaning of the “locusts” of Revelation 9, and they will have no idea. Some used to teach it represented the Lutherans, others demons, others something else, they don’t know. How can you claim to be the only interpreter, yet not interpret the Bible? We do not need the Catholic Church to understand Scripture, because the Bible itself teaches that God gives understanding to those who seek him diligently(Heb 11:6; Prov 2:6; Js 1:5). Scripture presents truth as something the Holy Spirit reveals to believers, not as something reserved only for one institutional interpreter (Jn 14:26; Jn 16:13; 1 Cor 2:12-14). Proverbs says that the LORD gives wisdom and understanding, and the NT says the Spirit teaches believers all things and guides them into truth (Prov 2:6; Jn 14:26;16:13). That means the deciding requirement for understanding Scripture is not membership in a particular church, but a humble heart, prayerful reading, and dependence on God (Ps 119:18; Js 1:5; Prov 3:5-6). The Bible also shows ordinary believers hearing, examining, and understanding God’s Word. In Acts, the Bereans were praised because they received the message eagerly and examined the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so (Acts 17:11). Paul tells Timothy that, FROM CHILDHOOD, the sacred writings are able to make one wise for salvation, and that Scripture is useful for teaching and training in righteousness (2 Tim 3:15-17). These passages imply that Scripture is clear enough for God’s people to be responsible readers, not so locked away that only one church can unlock it. This, however, does not mean every interpretation is equally good (2 Peter 3:16), but that the final authority is God speaking through His Word, and believers should approach it with prayer, humility, and obedience (2 Tim 3:16-17; Js 1:5; Jn 17:17). The Holy Spirit is able to correct error, convict the heart, and illuminate the meaning of Scripture to those who genuinely seek God (Jn 16:13; 1 Cor 2:12-14). So the argument is not: “I can interpret however I want,” but “I do not need a single human institution as the indispensable mediator of Scripture, because God Himself teaches His people” (Lk 24:45; Jn 17:17). Remember: “But the anointing which ye have received of him abideth in you, and ye need not that any man teach you: but as the same anointing teacheth you of all things, and is truth, and is no lie, and even as it hath taught you, ye shall abide in him.” (1 Jn 2:27 KJV).

26.x: It pleases God to use the humble and the fool to confound (shame) the strong: “But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty” (1 Cor 1:27 KJV). God deliberately selects what seems foolish or insignificant by human standards. Think of David, a shepherd boy defeating Goliath, or the apostles, uneducated fishermen leading the early church. This nullifies wisdom and displays divine power through unlike vessels. Deuteronomy 7:7-8 explains YHWH chose Israel not for their greatness but because they were the fewest of peoples, to proclaim His power through them. From slaves in Egypt, He delivered them with mighty acts like the Exodus plagues and Red Sea crossing, shaming the prideful mighty Egypt.

27.x: This verse highlights the unique intimacy between the authentic sinless man born of Mary and the divine Spirit, for the two are one (Jn 10:30). God is not known through human intellect alone, but through the person of Jesus. The “all things” suggests that MAN Jesus has been given total cosmic and redemptive authority since all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily in him (Col 2:8-9). To “know the Father” via the Son is to recognize that the Father is fully present in the Son: “he that hath seen me hath seen the Father” (Jn 14:9 KJV). As an omnipresent Spirit, we cannot see or understand God, but as an incarnate human being, the Son gives understanding of the Father as the image to the invisible Spirit (Heb 1:3). “No man hath seen God at any time, the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath DECLARED him.” (Jn 1:18 KJV). The word “declared” (Greek exēgēsato) means to explain, unfold, or make known. The Son is uniquely qualified because he is “in the bosom of the Father” (intimate direct knowledge). “And we know that the Son of God is come, and HATH GIVEN US AN UNDERSTANDING, that we may know him that is true, and we are in him that is true, even in his Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God, and eternal life” (1 Jn 5:20 KJV). The man Jesus is the Word of God made flesh, what Jesus says is what God the Father says: “For I have not spoken of myself; but the Father which sent me, he gave me a commandment, what I should say, and what I should speak.” (Jn 12:49 KJV). The Son makes the invisible God known: “Who is the image of the invisible God…” (Col 1:15 KJV). If you want to understand who God is, you look at the Son: his life, Words, and character are the explanation of the Father because he is the Father in the flesh. Trinitarias will be confused when they get to heaven looking for the Father. I have a feeling Jesus will reply to them the same way he did to Philip: “Philip saith unto him, Lord, show us the Father, and it sufficeth us. Jesus saith unto him, Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Show us the Father?” (Jn 14:8-9 KJV).

28.x: In the first-century contest, “laboring and heavy laden” referred to the crushing weight of the religious legalism imposed by the Pharisees. They had added hundreds of minute oral traditions to the Law of Moses, creating a burden that no one could keep. “Come to me”: Jesus shifts the focus from a system (the law-based requirements of the Pharisees) to a person (himself).

29.x: “Take my yoke”: A yoke is a wooden crosspiece or beam fastened over the necks of two draft animals, such as oxen, to harness them together for pulling a plow, cart, or heavy load evenly. In Jewish culture, a “yoke” symbolized a teacher’s interpretation of the law. To take a rabbi’s yoke was to commit to living by his specific rules. By offering his own yoke, Jesus is claiming to be the ultimate teacher whose interpretation of God’s will is not a burden, but a path to alignment with God. “Rest unto your souls”: This is not just physical relaxation. It refers to the deep spiritual peace that comes from being reconciled to God through faith rather than trying to earn salvation through works.

30.x: “my yoke is easy, and my burden is light”: The yoke also symbolizes servitude/slavery. Jesus assumes everyone is yoked to something, either to sin, legalism, or to him. We’re all enslaved to something, so what could possibly be better than becoming servants/slaves to what is good, God? The Pharisees’ legalism was a yoke that made people "weary and heavy laden." Following Jesus is easier because He's "meek and lowly," we're not striving alone, and his righteousness is imputed to us. It is peaceful when you realize salvation is not based on our own efforts but on the works of Christ on the cross. There is no specific amount of works one has to do to enter heaven, everyone will produce different amounts of works based on Jesus’ plan, not our own: “Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine… I am the vine, ye are the branches… for without me ye can do nothing.” (Jn 15:4-5 KJV). We are a branch, and a branch has no independent life- its fruit comes from the vine’s life flowing through it. Likewise, spiritual fruit is the result of Christ’s life working in us, not just human effort. So the starting point is “abiding”: staying connected, dependent, and receptive to Christ. To “abide” in Jesus is to follow his Word (Jn 15:7). His teaching shapes your thinking, decisions, and desires. “Continue ye in my love… If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love…” (Jn 15:9-10). Obedience is not how you earn fruit, but how you remain in the place where His life flows freely through you. “without me ye can do nothing” (John 15:5): This cuts against the idea that you can produce spiritual fruit by willpower alone (by being yoked to a religious system). Abiding is a posture of reliance: prayer, trust, surrender. If you abide, the fruits will be made manifest: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance…” (Gal 5:22-23 KJV) & “Being filled with the fruits of righteousness, which are by Jesus Christ…” (Phil 1:11 KJV) - Notice: “by Jesus Christ” - he is always the source.

Jesus is our new Sabbath. In the OT Law, the 4th Commandment of God required the Jews to rest on the Sabbath. The NT teaches that the physical Sabbath of the OT was a shadow (a preview) and Christ is the substance (the reality). Paul writes: “Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.” (Col 2:16-17 KJV). Hence, the seventh-day Sabbath was designed to remind Israel that God rested from creation and to trust Him for their provision (Ex 20:8-11). It was a requirement for the Old Covenant. However, since humans could never truly “rest” from their sin or achieve perfection through the law, they needed a savior. Jesus fulfills the purpose of the Sabbath - which is to stop trying to justify yourself and trust in God’s completed work. Most Christians (except Seventh-day Adventist and some others) teach that we are no longer under the ceremonial aspects of the Mosaic Law (it is the only Commandment from the 10 Commandments that changed) due to: (1) Christ is the fulfillment: Just as animal sacrifices are no longer needed because Christ was the ultimate sacrifice, teh weekly Sabbath rest is no longer a legal requirement because we have found “soul-rest” in his finished work on the cross. (2) Hebrews 4:9-10 states: “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his.” This suggests that the true Sabbath is a state of living by faith rather than a specific calendar day. (3) New Covenant Freedom: In the NT, the focus shifts from a day of the week to a life of devotion. Paul emphasizes that the believer is free to treat every day as unto the Lord: “One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind. He that regardeth the day, regardeth it unto the Lord; and he that regardeth not the day, to the Lord he doth not regard it…” (Rom 14:5-6 KJV). Hence, keeping a “literal” Sabbath is no longer a tool to gain favor with God; instead, Jesus is the actual rest we occupy 24/7. We “keep” the Sabbath by consistently placing our trust in him Him to sustain our lives and justify our souls, rather than relying on our own “works” to prove our righteousness.

2-3.x: John was imprisoned by Herod Antipas because he publicly denounced Herod’s marriage to Herodias(his niece) as unlawful and immoral, and because Herod feared John’s growing influence over the people (Lk 3:19-20). For a man of the wilderness, the “darkness” and confinement were likely crushing. John began to doubt. He had preached that the Messiah would come with “fan and fire” to judge the wicked (Mt 3:11-12). Instead, he hears that Jesus is eating with sinners and healing the sick, while Herod remains on the throne and John remains in chains. “He that should come”: In the OT, the one who was prophesied to come and save His people was YHWH Himself: “behold, your God will come with vengeance.. He will come and save you” (Isa 35:4 KJV). The very next verses describe the blind seeing and the lame leaping - the exact list Jesus gives John. Jesus is telling John: “I am the God who Isaiah said would come.” He is the Father (the invisible Spirit of YHWH) dwelling in and acting through the Son (the human body).

4-5.x: Jesus doesn’t give a simple “Yes” or “No.” Instead, he points to his works. This list is a direct “ID card” of the Messiah based on the prophecies of Isaiah: (1) “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped. Then shall the lame man leap as an hart, and the tongue of the dumb sing: for in the wilderness shall waters break out, and streams in the desert.” (Isa 35:5-6 KJV); (2) “The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me; because the Lord hath anointed me to preach good tidings unto the meek; he hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound” (Isa 61:1 KJV). “the poor have the gospel preached to them”: In the ancient world, the “poor” were often ignored by religious elites. Jesus highlights that the gospel reaching the marginalized is as much a miracle as the blind seeing. When Jesus tells John’s disciples to report what they “see and hear,” he is directing them to witness the Deity within him. The humanity of Jesus was the “veil”, but the works of Jesus were the “glory” of the Father shining through. John was looking for the “Father” to come in judgement (Mt 3:2,10-12; Lk 3:3,16-17), as he was preparing the way for the LORD(YHWH) (Mt 3:3). Jesus’ answer subtly reminds John that the “Father” has indeed come, but He has come in the form of the “Son” to bring mercy first. The “Sonship” was the role God took to suffer and heal; the “Fatherhood” is the divine power that makes those healings possible.

7-8.x: Jesus turns to the crowd after John’s disciples depart. He begins to defend John’s character and clarify his unique role in history, ensuring that the people do not mistake John’s moment of doubt for a lack of strength. “A reed shaken with the wind?”: A reed by the Jordan River is easily blown by any breeze. Jesus is saying John was not a “flip-flopper” or a man who changed his message to please the crowds. He was a man of steel, deep in his convictions. “A man clothed in soft raiment?”: John didn’t wear luxury silks or live in palaces. If the people wanted comfort and political polish, they wouldn’t have gone to the desert to find it.

9-10.x: John was “more than a prophet.” He was unique because he didn’t just point to a future Messiah; he physically introduced him. Then Jesus quotes Malachi 3:1. By doing so, he identifies John as the “Messenger” and himself as YHWH, the LORD who was promised to come to His temple.

16-17.x: Jesus compares the people to children playing in the marketplace. In their game, one group tries to start a “wedding” by playing the flute, but the other group refuses to dance. Then they try to play “funeral” by wailing, but the others refuse to mourn. The point is that people were impossible to please. They weren’t looking for truth; they were looking for an excuse to remain uncommitted.

18-19.x: Jesus then applies the parable to himself and John the Baptist to show that no matter the “tune” God played, the people refused to join in. This verse also shows that Christians are not called to the same outward style of holiness. John the Baptist lived with strong self-denial, while Jesus did not, and Jesus’ point is that people wrongly judged both of them instead of recognizing God’s wisdom in each calling. Some believers may be drawn to stricter disciplines like fasting, simplicity, or celibacy, while others serve God faithfully in a more ordinary pattern of life; neither automatically makes someone more or less Christian. What matters is obedience to God, not looking severe or impressive outwardly. This passage warns against confusing external style with spiritual reality, because both John’s abstinence and Jesus’ table fellowship could be misunderstood by people who were unwilling to accept God’s wisdom. “Wisdom is justified of her children”: There is a variant here. The CT (two oldest mss) has “works,” while the TR(almost identical with MT, but with some Latin influence) and the MT(majority of mss) have “children.” The variant, however, does not affect the meaning: wisdom is proven right by its results. John’s ministry produced repentance. Jesus’ ministry produced salvation and transformed lives.Even if the “generation” complained and called names, the actual fruit of John’s and Jesus’ ministries proved they were both sent by God. Jesus is exposing the hypocrisy of indifference. If you don’t want to believe, any excuse will do. If the prophet is serious, he’s “too intense.” If the Savior is joyful, he’s “too worldly.” Jesus is warning that the problem isn’t the messenger or the message: it’s the heart of the listener.

21-22.x: Tyre and Sidon were Gentile (pagan) coastal cities known for their pride and idolatry, often condemned by OT prophets. Jesus asserts that these “heathen” cities would have put on sackcloth and ashes (traditional signs of deep mourning and repentance) if they had seen what Chorazin and Bethsaida saw. Because the Galilean cities had more light (the presence of Christ), the judgement would be more tolerable for the pagans than for them.
